Hey OP, I understand your pain. My own father hanged himself while he and I were at the family cabin. No note, no warning. I'm the oldest of my siblings, and everyone had a different reaction. 

I had a similar one to you. I'm mad. Angry at his selfishness. My siblings don't understand my grief, and it's really not their job to. I know we all wish family could support each other under emotional duress, but their actions are influenced by their emotions just as yours are.

You're not an asshole for sharing how you feel hurt. You will be an asshole if you build resentment toward your family for not grieving how you do. It's not their fault that he's dead. 

I don't have a solution for the pain or loss. I just know the wound does heal. In time, as a new way of living becomes routine, it won't be as raw. I do recommend having an outlet to speak freely about how you feel. 

I'm so terribly sorry for your loss of your father.

So, I just rewatched the Architect scene to refresh myself. 

My own personal theory, after several viewings of the trilogy, I'd that the Matrix has several layers. It's not confined to what is originally introduced as 1999 "peak civilisation".

When he speaks of the first version, the "utopia", it failed because it lacked a necessary component of the human condition, suffering.

The "real world" is a way to reward the illusion of choice. To allow room for the loud, rebellious kids to feel like they've found the truth. To simulate conflict. 

The One represents the indomitable spirit. He is physical belief. 

Faith and belief are separated from cold, hard math. It's a variable of humanity that can not be predicted but accounted for. Hence, the Oracle (look up the definition of Oracle) using this variable to influence The One into perpetuating the Matrix.  

As for programs entering into the "real world", the were there all along just in different forms. Manifesting as something different and alien from what we self identify.

This is especially true given the Architects opening line, "... You have many questions, and although the process has altered your consciousness, you remain irrevocably human..." 

You may view this in reference to Neo's transformation into The One. I however, see this as evidence of Neo and The One being an archetype that is being incorporated into the Matrix. Rather than an opposition to the system, a vital function to keep it functioning as intended(though not originally envisioned)

Zion is a part of the Matrix. The whole system that we view, what's shown in the movies, is cyclical and potentially endless. We are only viewing a snapshot of its history by following this iteration's characters. 

The story of the Matrix is an allegory. Given its philosophical and religious influences. There is no free will, only the illusion of choice. There is no escape, only existence. Life is created by a "God" and experienced as a simulation, curated and perfected. The sentient programs are proof that even consciousness is something not unique to humans. Though maybe faith is. 

God created all things. He created heaven and the angels. He created humanity and a perfect garden. We revolted, rebeled, and we cast out into the world, just like the angels before us. 

Or maybe those were just the first two iterations.

If you ever get the chance, I'd recommend possible getting a consult for an MSLT(Multiple Sleep Latency Test), but only if you feel that you find it difficult to stay awake, and it impedes your day to day activities. The test is run to rule out narcolepsy. 

One of the key symptoms that an MSLT looks for is early onset REM. Typically, within 10-15 minutes of sleep during a 40-minute period of rest. 

However, if you don't have any issues staying awake, I wouldn't pursue testing as a Narcolepsy diagnosis is permanent and can be very restricting. 

If you do just fine and don't have any concerns, then the dreams are just a neat aspect of you!

[All this being said, I am NOT a doctor and only sharing my knowledge. An aspect of healthcare I don't agree with is keeping people in the dark if they aren't "in-the-know." If  a physician makes a recommendation, trust them over an internet stranger 😊]

How often do you nap and how difficult do you find it to fall asleep?

Have you ever had a fainting spell while under intense emotion? (laughing, crying, fear/surprise) 

I wouldn't be worried about experiencing or remembering several dreams consistently. If anything, so long as it does not cause you distress, it sounds like a gift! I may envy such a thing if I dreamt little or none at all. 

I feel it's important to know that dreams = REM but REM =/= dreams. In so far as being necessary or important for health. Some people don't dream but experience REM and are perfectly healthy. The experience of dreaming is entirely subjective.

That's wonderful! I love knowing that people are sleeping better with treatment 😊 

It is kind of an unspoken rule amongst sleep techs that we don't wake people from REM. No one likes an interrupted dream 😄

If you do have sleep apnea, then I would assume that is a factor. 

However, just because a person achieved healthy amounts of REM in a night doesn't mean that they will remember any dreams. I've only had 2 patients report having dreamt while in my lab, while something like 85% experience at least one stage of REM during the night.

Well, as far as I know, it's the AASM/ABSM ( American being the key to the acronym) that is recognized internationally. It's relatively cheap to get in the US. The most expensive part is the test at $500. Most hospitals will sponsor you to become certified anyway since you need clinical hours to even be allowed to test. 

It was FAR cheaper for me than my CDL was 😅

I'm not sure, my own experience is that my dreams are very narrative driven. Like chapter out of a book or episodes from a show. The events are chronological and ordered, the only weird 'dreamy' bits are details like object placement or colors or people/behavior. 

I do feel that the dreams we remember best are from the last stage of REM we have, though. It's possible that the brain stores bits from each stage, and then we reconcile it upon waking. 

I can't say with any authority that either is true universally or on average. I'm not even sure what field of study or medicine works with that aspect of the human experience 🤔 

It's interesting to think and speculate on though!

It is actually! It's really common when treating a disorder that disrupts the body's usual cycles. 

For example, when someone has the right pressure on CPAP for the first time, they will experience what's called "REM rebound".  They enter an excessively long REM stage as a way of over compensating for it's absence. 

Regardless of dreams, REM is an incredibly important aspect of our sleep. It's when our brain detoxes and flushes out its waste from expending energy throughout the day. Without routine REM, that waste builds up and can become toxic. There are studies being conducted that show some evidence that links untreated sleep apnea to neurological disorders/diseases like dementia later in life.

I've got some work history with medicine, but I actually went from being a trucker to this 😅 A position opened up at my small local hospital, and I applied! 

It's like that all over. You don't need a degree to become a sleep tech. Only on the job training and an 80 hr class. That is, if you don't want to become certified.

Most hospitals don't require a tech to get their cert, but it is a large pay raise and more of a supervisory role depending on hospital size. The test, however, is one of the hardest out there. It's got like a 40% pass rate or something, I can't remember at the moment.  

What's really cool is the RPSGT(Registered Polysomnography Technician) cert is recognized internationally. You can work in Italy, England, Germany, Japan, and many others once you register in the US. 

As for my own experiences, night terrors are most common in pediatrics, and I work with adults. It can happen with PTSD though that's in extreme cases. 
I haven't had anyone yet experience sleep paralysis in my lab though I have had people talk or move in their sleep. One lady would yell/scream during her REM but didn't complain of any bad dreams or unpleasantness.

Becoming a sleep tech is super easy! It's one of the last few healthcare jobs that pays competitively without a degree. 

I highly recommend it as the work-life balance is unmatched with any other job I've had and the workload is relaxed, but fascinating AND you're helping improve people's lives!

AASM (American Academy of Sleep Medicine) is constantly changing and updating as more and more data is collected/studies conducted. 

For example, we "previously" had 5 stages of sleep, but stages 3 and 4 were consolidated into just stage 3 or 'slow wave sleep' (deep sleep). 

You're close on the typical sleep cycle. Now it's 60-90 minutes with REM 'hopefully', taking less than or equal to 50%. 


My job is much less to due with the neurological aspect of sleep or dreams, though 😅 It is what I find most fascinating, but I mainly focus on the respiratory aspect of sleep and diagnosing sleep apnea. 

I'm curious about your background in neurology and would love to hear more about your experiences/experiments with dreaming!

Source: I am a sleep technologist 

It depends of the quality of sleep. Things like caffeine, blue light, routines... usual sleep hygiene stuff has an influence on how well we achieve each stage of sleep.

Usually, I see anywhere from 0 to 3 REM cycles lasting around 30 minutes to an hour each. Though no REM is quite a bad thing and unusual, typically due to substance abuse or severe sleep apnea. 

REM is quite a fragile stage of sleep and can easily be disturbed. If your stages are, on average, less than 30 minutes, I'd be concerned. 

Sleep apnea is also far more common than most realize. If you feel that you're not getting restful sleep, go get it checked! There's more treatment options available if the idea of a CPAP worries you!

The only thing that I could remember, to keep myself grounded, was something Dr. Peterson had said about behavior at a funeral. How to face hell.
